sceneHappening: The Feast of Booths in Jerusalem: crowds divided, and rivers of living water
summary: After these things Jesus walks in Galilee, because he does not want to walk in Judea, since the Jews seek to kill him. The Jews' feast of Booths is at hand, and his brothers say, "Depart from here, and go into Judea, that your disciples also may see your works which you do. For no one does anything in secret, while he himself seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world." John adds that even his brothers did not believe in him. Jesus says, "My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready. The world can't hate you, but it hates me, because I testify about it, that its works are evil. You go up to the feast. I am not yet going up to this feast, because my time is not yet fulfilled." After his brothers have gone up, he goes up too, not publicly but in secret. At the feast the Jews look for him and ask, "Where is he?" and there is much murmuring about him among the crowds: some say, "He is a good man," others, "He leads the people astray." About the middle of the feast Jesus goes up into the temple and teaches. The Jews marvel, "How does this man know letters, having never been educated?" Jesus says, "My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I speak from myself." He asks, "Why do you seek to kill me?" The crowd answers, "You have a demon! Who seeks to kill you?" He says, "I did one work, and you all marvel because of it. ... Don't judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment." Some of the people of Jerusalem say, "Isn't this he whom they seek to kill? Behold, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Can it be that the rulers indeed know that this is truly the Christ? However we know where this man comes from, but when the Christ comes, no one will know where he comes from." Jesus cries out in the temple, "You both know me, and know where I am from. I have not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you don't know. I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me." They seek to seize him, but no one lays a hand on him, because his hour has not yet come. Many of the crowd believe in him: "When the Christ comes, will he do more signs than these which this man has done?" The Pharisees hear the crowd murmuring and send officers to arrest him. Jesus says, "I will be with you a little while longer, then I go to him who sent me. You will seek me, and won't find me; and where I am, you can't come." On the last day, the great day of the feast, Jesus stands and cries out, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink! He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water." John explains, "But he said this about the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive. For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn't yet glorified." The crowd is divided: "This is truly the prophet," "This is the Christ," and others, "What, does the Christ come out of Galilee? Hasn't the Scripture said that the Christ comes of the seed of David, and from Bethlehem, the village where David was?" The officers return without arresting him: "No man ever spoke like this man!" The Pharisees answer, "You aren't also led astray, are you? Have any of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees? But this multitude, who don't know the law, are accursed." Nicodemus, he who came to him by night, being one of them, says, "Does our law judge a man, unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?" They answer, "Are you also from Galilee? Search, and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee."
whySettingMatters: The Feast of Booths (Sukkot) fell in the autumn, and pilgrims lived in leafy shelters for a week to remember the wilderness (Leviticus 23:33-43). It was the greatest of the festivals and the one most associated with water, as the people prayed for rain, and with light; later Jewish sources describe a daily water-pouring ceremony and the lighting of great lamps in the temple courts, which gives background to Jesus' cry about water here and his "I am the light of the world" in chapter 8, though how much of that ritual existed in Jesus' day is debated. "The last day, the great day" was the seventh or an added eighth day. The "rivers of living water" saying cites a Scripture that isn't clear; Zechariah 14:8, Ezekiel 47, Isaiah 58:11, and Psalm 78:16 have all been proposed. Whether the water flows from the believer or from Jesus depends on how the punctuation is read, and is debated. John explains the water as the Spirit. His brothers' advice shows the pressure to make a public display, and Jesus' answers about "time" (kairos) and "hour" are John's way of saying events happen on the Father's schedule. The people's belief that no one will know where the Christ comes from and the Pharisees' that no prophet comes from Galilee both overlook his birth in Bethlehem. The Pharisees call the crowd "accursed" for not knowing the law, and Nicodemus quietly objects on legal grounds, appealing to due process.

people.note: Goes up to the feast in secret, teaches openly, and invites the thirsty.
His brothers, who do not yet believe in him.
The Judean authorities who are trying to kill him.
Return without him: "No man ever spoke like this man!"

questions: Jesus' brothers tell him to go public, and he says his time hasn't come. What does he mean by "time"?
On the last day of the feast, Jesus cries out about thirst. Why might he choose that moment?
The crowd, the officers, and the Pharisees all give different answers about who he is. What does each assume?
Nicodemus speaks up, but quietly. What does his move cost him, and what does it show?
